title: How many trades until skill shows?
objectives: Use the central limit theorem to judge whether an average return is real
Compute a standard error, a $t$-ratio and a Sharpe ratio's standard error
Explain why many tests and short records mislead

screens.title: Two track records
screens.prose: Two traders show you their records. A traded for 3 months, B for 4 years. Their daily returns are equally noisy.
screens.question: Whose average would be harder for a trader with no skill to match by luck?

options.text: B's, despite the smaller average
A's, because 0.12% is twice 0.06%
options.why: You compared the averages alone. Over 63 noisy days a big average comes easily; over 1,008 days it does not.

options.text: Equally hard, since the daily sd is the same
options.why: The same daily noise averages out far more over 1,008 days than over 63.

options.text: There is no way to tell without the full distribution
options.why: The mean and sd are enough here, as the next screens show.

hints.text: Which average is built from more days?
Noise in an average shrinks like $1/\sqrt n$. Which record has more days to shrink it?

feedback.correct: Four years of data make a small average hard to fake.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh the length of each record, not just its average.

explain.text: Luck moves a 63-day average a lot and a 1,008-day average very little. We will measure each record against the luck it could contain. A's turns out to be ordinary; B's is not.

screens.title: The spread of luck
screens.prose: Picture a trader with no skill: true mean 0, daily sd 1%. The curve is their average over $n$ days. The shaded tail is the chance of averaging 0.12% or more.

derive.caption: $n = {{n}}$ days: sd of the average $= 1\% / \sqrt{n} = {{fixed(1 / sqrt(n), 3)}}\%$

screens.question: Set $n = 63$. Roughly how often does this no-skill trader average 0.12% or more?

options.text: About 17% of the time
Almost never
options.why: That is the picture at 1,000 days or more. At 63 days the curve is still wide.

options.text: About half the time
options.why: Half the curve lies above 0, not above 0.12%. Read the shaded tail.

options.text: About 5% of the time
options.why: Read the label at $n = 63$ exactly; 5% needs a longer record.

hints.text: Slide $n$ to 63 and read the shaded probability.
The label shows $P(\bar X \ge 0.12)$ for the current $n$.

feedback.correct: At 63 days, luck alone gives 0.12% or more about one time in six.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to 63 days and read the label.

explain.text: At 63 days the sd of the average is $1\% / \sqrt{63} \approx 0.126\%$. This sd of an average has a name: the **standard error**, $\sigma / \sqrt n$. A's 0.12% is less than one standard error, so it is ordinary luck.

screens.title: Count the standard errors
screens.prose: B averaged 0.06% a day over 1,008 days, with daily sd 1%. B's standard error is $1\% / \sqrt{1008} \approx 0.0315\%$.
screens.question: How many standard errors above zero is B's average? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Divide the average by the standard error.

byKey.inverse: You divided the standard error by the average. Put the average on top.
byKey.sd: You divided by the daily sd, 1%. Use the standard error of the average.
byKey.A: That is A's ratio, $0.12/0.126$. Use B's numbers.

explain.text: B's average is $1.90$ standard errors above zero; A's was $0.95$. A no-skill trader beats 1.9 standard errors only about 3% of the time. Length of record, not size of average, carried the evidence.

canvas.caption: No-skill chance of 0.06% or more over 1,008 days: about 0.028

screens.title: How many days until skill shows?
screens.prose: Now suppose a strategy truly earns 0.05% a day with sd 1%. The curve is two standard errors, $2\sigma / \sqrt n$, against days $n$. Skill shows once the true mean clears that line.
screens.question: Slide $n$ until two standard errors equal the true mean of 0.05%.

hints.text: Watch the caption: stop when it reads 0.05%.
The dot must sit on the dashed line.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Stop where the dot meets the dashed line.

byKey.early: Two standard errors are still above 0.05%. A real 0.05% edge cannot yet be told from luck.
byKey.late: You went past the crossing. Two standard errors fall to 0.05% at 1,600 days.

explain.text: Two standard errors fall to 0.05% when $\sqrt n = 2\sigma/\mu = 40$, so $n = 1{,}600$ days. At 252 trading days a year, that is about 6.3 years. A genuine, decent edge takes years to prove.

screens.title: The t-ratio
screens.prose: Each time you divided an average by its standard error. That is the $t$-ratio: $$t = \frac{\bar X}{\sigma / \sqrt n} = \frac{\bar X \sqrt n}{\sigma}.$$ If the true mean is 0, the central limit theorem makes $t$ close to $N(0, 1)$. So $|t| > 2$ by luck has chance about 0.0455.
screens.question: A strategy shows $t = 2.5$ over 500 days. What does that tell you?

options.text: Luck alone rarely gives a $t$ this large
There is a 99% chance the strategy has skill
options.why: You turned the chance of the data given no skill into a chance of skill. That swap is the prosecutor's fallacy.

options.text: The true mean is 2.5 times the daily sd
options.why: $t$ counts standard errors, not daily sds. The mean itself may be tiny.

options.text: The next 500 days will also give $t$ near 2.5
options.why: A new sample gives a new $t$. Even a real edge produces a spread of $t$ values.

hints.text: Under no skill, $t$ is roughly $N(0, 1)$. How often does that exceed 2.5?

feedback.correct: A $t$ of 2.5 is unusual for luck alone, about one time in 160.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read $t$ as a count of standard errors under no skill.

explain.text: With no skill, $P(t > 2.5) \approx 0.006$. That is a statement about the data assuming no skill. It is not the chance the strategy has skill; that needs a prior, as Bayes' rule showed.

screens.title: The Sharpe ratio and its error
screens.prose: Daily returns have mean $\mu$ and sd $\sigma$, independent across 252 trading days a year. We record $T$ years.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: A year's return has mean $252\mu$, by linearity of expectation
and sd $\sqrt{252}\,\sigma$, since 252 independent daily variances add
So the annualised Sharpe ratio is $SR = \dfrac{252\mu}{\sqrt{252}\,\sigma} = \dfrac{\mu\sqrt{252}}{\sigma}$
With $n = 252T$ days, $t = \dfrac{\bar X \sqrt n}{\sigma} = \dfrac{\bar X\sqrt{252}}{\sigma}\sqrt T = \widehat{SR}\,\sqrt T$
$t$ has sd about 1, so $\widehat{SR} = t / \sqrt T$ has standard error about $1 / \sqrt T$

hints.text: Build the yearly mean and sd first.
Mean, sd, Sharpe, then rewrite $t$ with $n = 252T$, then divide by $\sqrt T$.

feedback.correct: Annualise, form the Sharpe ratio, link it to $t$, then read off its error.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from a year's mean and sd.

byKey.sr: The Sharpe ratio needs the yearly mean and sd first.
byKey.se: The standard error comes last, once $\widehat{SR}$ is tied to $t$.

explain.text: For 0.05% a day with sd 1%, $SR = 0.05 \times \sqrt{252} \approx 0.79$. Its standard error after $T$ years is about $1/\sqrt T$. So $t = SR\sqrt T$ reaches 2 at $T = (2/0.79)^2 \approx 6.3$ years, as the slider showed.

screens.title: A big average is not a big Sharpe
screens.prose: Two strategies ran for one year. P averaged 0.20% a day with daily sd 4%. Q averaged 0.05% a day with daily sd 0.5%.
screens.question: After one year, which record is stronger evidence of skill?

options.text: Q's: its Sharpe ratio is twice P's
P's: it earns four times as much a day
options.why: You compared averages. P's average is buried in 4% daily noise; Q's sits clear of its 0.5% noise.

options.text: Equal, since both ran for one year
options.why: Equal length is not equal evidence. Evidence is $t = SR\sqrt T$, and the Sharpe ratios differ.

options.text: Neither can be judged after a year
options.why: One year is short, but $t$ still ranks them: about 0.8 for P and 1.6 for Q.

hints.text: Compute each Sharpe ratio: mean over sd, times $\sqrt{252} \approx 15.87$.

feedback.correct: Q's Sharpe ratio is about 1.59; P's is about 0.79.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide each mean by its own sd before comparing.

byKey.P: You compared averages. P's average is buried in 4% daily noise; Q's sits clear of its 0.5% noise.

explain.text: $SR_P = 0.05 \times 15.87 \approx 0.79$ and $SR_Q = 0.1 \times 15.87 \approx 1.59$. With $T = 1$, $t = SR$, so Q is at 1.6 standard errors and P at 0.8. Neither clears 2 yet.

screens.title: Twenty tries at luck
screens.prose: A researcher backtests 20 independent strategies, none of which has any skill. Each $t$-ratio is then close to $N(0, 1)$, so each has chance 0.0455 of $|t| > 2$.

state.caption: Each tail beyond 2 has chance 0.0228; both together 0.0455

screens.question: What is the chance at least one of the 20 shows $|t| > 2$? Give 3 decimal places.

hints.text: Find the chance that none of them does, then take it from 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the chance all 20 stay inside $\pm 2$, then subtract from 1.

byKey.added: You added 20 chances of 0.0455. That double-counts the cases where two or more pass.
byKey.one: That is for one strategy. With 20 tries the chance of a fluke grows.
byKey.all: That is the chance all 20 pass. The question asks about at least one.

explain.text: With 20 tries, a 2-sigma fluke turns up 61% of the time. Report the best of 20 and luck looks like skill. Count every strategy you tested before you trust the winner.

screens.title: A two-year track record
screens.prose: A fund shows an annualised Sharpe ratio of 1.0. The shaded band is the estimate plus or minus two standard errors, $1.0 \pm 2/\sqrt T$. Slide the length of the record $T$.
screens.question: The fund's record is 2 years long. What can you conclude?

options.text: The Sharpe ratio is not distinguishable from 0 at 95%
It is clearly skill, since a Sharpe ratio of 1 is excellent
options.why: You judged the size alone. At $T = 2$ the band runs from about $-0.41$ to $2.41$, and it contains 0.

options.text: The true Sharpe ratio is 1.0
options.why: The record only estimates it. The band shows the truth could be far from 1.0.

options.text: Nothing at all, since 2 years tells us nothing
options.why: Two years does narrow things: the band excludes a Sharpe ratio of 3, say.

hints.text: Set $T = 2$ and check whether 0 is inside the band.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. At $T = 2$, look at where the band starts.

explain.text: The standard error is $1/\sqrt 2 \approx 0.71$, so $t \approx 1.41$ and the band reaches below 0. Slide to $T = 4$: the band starts at exactly 0. A Sharpe ratio of 1.0 needs about 4 years to clear 2 standard errors.

screens.title: A real edge, a losing year
screens.prose: A £10m book earns £5,000 a day on average, with daily sd £100,000. Days are independent; a year has 252 of them. Use $\Phi(-0.794) = 0.2136$.
screens.question: What is the chance this book loses money over a year?

hints.text: Zero is $1.26 / 1.587 \approx 0.794$ sds below the mean.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the year's mean and sd, then standardise 0.

byKey.days: That is the chance of a losing day, $\Phi(-0.05)$. A year adds 252 days.
byKey.no-scale: You kept the daily sd of £100,000 for the whole year. Variances add, so the year's sd is $\sqrt{252}$ times larger.
byKey.upper: That is the chance of a winning year. Take the lower tail.

explain.text: The year's P&L has mean £1.26m and sd £1.59m, so a losing year has chance about 0.21. This book's Sharpe ratio is 0.79, a real edge. Even so, one year in five is a loss.

ideas: The standard error of an average is $\sigma / \sqrt n$; the $t$-ratio $\bar X\sqrt n / \sigma$ counts how many of them the average is from 0.
To show a true mean $\mu$ at two standard errors needs $n = (2\sigma/\mu)^2$ days: 1,600 for 0.05% against 1%.
An annualised Sharpe ratio has standard error about $1/\sqrt T$, so $t = SR\sqrt T$; many tries make 2-sigma flukes common.

formula.name: Skill or luck
formula.tex: t = \dfrac{\bar X\sqrt n}{\sigma} = SR\,\sqrt T, \qquad SE(\widehat{SR}) \approx \dfrac{1}{\sqrt T}
formula.note: With no skill, $t \approx N(0, 1)$, so $|t| > 2$ has chance about 0.0455.

summary.trap: A high average over a short or noisy record is weak evidence. Judge the Sharpe ratio and the length together.

quiz.prose: A strategy's daily returns have sd 1.5%.
quiz.question: What is the standard error of its average daily return over 400 days? Give a percentage.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the daily sd by $\sqrt{400}$.

byKey.over-n: You divided by 400. The standard error uses $\sqrt n$.
byKey.sd: That is the daily sd. The average of 400 days is far less noisy.

quiz.prose: A strategy shows an annualised Sharpe ratio of 2.0 over its first 3 months, so $T = 0.25$ years.
quiz.question: How many standard errors from zero is that?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the Sharpe ratio by $\sqrt T$.

byKey.times-T: You divided by $\sqrt T$. Evidence grows with $\sqrt T$, so multiply.
byKey.raw: That is the Sharpe ratio itself. Over 3 months its standard error is $1/\sqrt{0.25} = 2$.

explain.text: The standard error of the Sharpe ratio is $1/\sqrt{0.25} = 2$, as large as the estimate. A Sharpe of 2 over 3 months is one standard error: easily luck.

quiz.prose: A strategy has a true annualised Sharpe ratio of 0.5.
quiz.question: About how many years until its expected $t$-ratio reaches 2?

byKey.half: You solved $2 \times 0.5 = T$. Use $t = SR\sqrt T$.

explain.text: $t = SR\sqrt T$, so $T = (2/0.5)^2 = 16$ years. Modest edges are very slow to prove.

quiz.prose: A no-skill strategy has $t$ close to $N(0, 1)$. Use $\Phi(2) = 0.9772$.
quiz.question: What is the chance it shows $t > 2$, an apparent positive edge?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the upper tail beyond 2.

byKey.both: That counts both tails. Only $t > 2$ is asked.

explain.text: $P(t > 2) = 1 - \Phi(2) = 0.0228$: about one no-skill strategy in 44 looks good by luck.
